articles.title: Make the whole car matte black
articles.summary: Put one zone over the car paint, give it a Matte base and a solid black colour, and keep it off the numbers and sponsors with Restrict to layers. Check the G ROUGH view: matte should be bright.
articles.what: A deadly flat black is the simplest look and a good first test of the colour and finish controls. The key is to set the colour yourself: a plain finish takes the colour you choose under BASE COLOR, while a finish that brings its own colour would ignore it.
when: You want a stealth, flat black car.
You want a matte base to put bright accents on.
how: Open your layered template, switch the template layers off, and press + Add Zone.

Under COLOR choose Remaining (everything no zone above has claimed), or press PICK COLOR FROM CAR and click the body colour. On a layered template also tick Car Paint under RESTRICT TO LAYERS so numbers and sponsors stay untouched.
Under BASE press Base Material, open the FOUNDATIONS category, then the Foundation Bases shelf, and choose Matte (or Primer, or Flat Black for the deadest look).
Set BASE COLOR to Use solid color and pick black (a very dark grey like 0a0a0a keeps a little shape).
Look at the live preview, then open the G ROUGH view under it: matte reads bright (roughness near 200). Open B COAT: it should not be at 16.
If it looks too dead, switch to Satin for a soft sheen, or keep the matte body and add gloss accents in a zone above it.
Press RENDER, then Ctrl+R in iRacing.

controls.effect: Opens the finish picker for the zone.

controls.label: BASE COLOR
controls.effect: Where the colour comes from; pick Use solid color for exact black.

controls.label: RESTRICT TO LAYERS
controls.effect: Keeps the zone off numbers and sponsors.

tips: Matte is roughness 200 and coat 160; Flat Black is roughness 250 and coat 255, the deadest.
To keep your own colours and only make them matte, set BASE COLOR to Use source paint (spec only).
pitfalls: Solid black over chrome zones above it does nothing: the higher zone wins.
Matte black hides paint flaws no more than gloss, but it hides reflections; judge it in the sim.

deep.heading: Why the colour is set by hand
deep.body: A plain finish takes the colour you choose under BASE COLOR, while a finish that brings its own colour would ignore it. That is why Matte (a plain foundation with no texture: roughness 200, coat 160) plus Use solid color is the clean way to get an exact black.

deep.heading: Matte in the shine views
deep.body: Matte reads bright in G ROUGH (roughness near 200) and the B COAT view should not be at 16, which is the glossiest. If the car looks too dead, Satin gives a soft sheen, or keep the matte body and add gloss accents in a zone above it.

deep.heading: Order of zones
deep.body: A solid black zone under a chrome zone does nothing: the higher zone wins. Put the black zone where it is meant to apply.

faq.q: Which matte should I pick?
faq.a: Matte is the standard flat finish (roughness 200, coat 160), Primer is a touch flatter, and Flat Black (roughness 250, coat 255) is the deadest.

faq.q: How do I check it is matte?
faq.a: Open G ROUGH under the preview: matte reads bright, with roughness near 200.

faq.q: Will it paint over my numbers?
faq.a: Not if you tick Car Paint under RESTRICT TO LAYERS.

faq.q: Does matte black hide flaws?
faq.a: It hides reflections, not flaws. Judge it in the sim.

mistakes.fix: Drag the black zone above it.

mistakes.fix: Use a plain foundation and set BASE COLOR to Use solid color.

articles.title: Chrome with your source colours (spec only)
articles.summary: A Foundation chrome with BASE COLOR set to Use source paint changes only the shine map and leaves your paint exactly as it is. Use it when you want your livery to be metallic, not repainted silver.
articles.what: The ordinary chrome base repaints the zone silver. A Foundation finish is a pure spec: it writes the metal and roughness and keeps your colours. This is how you make an existing livery chrome, satin chrome or metallic without touching the art, numbers or sponsors.
when: You want your finished livery to be shiny chrome without changing the colours.
You want satin or brushed metal over your paint.
how: Open your paint and press + Add Zone. Cover the area you want: Remaining for the whole car, or PICK COLOR FROM CAR on one colour.
Under BASE press Base Material, open the FOUNDATIONS category, then the Foundation Bases shelf, and choose Chrome or Satin Chrome (softer).
Set BASE COLOR to Use source paint (spec only).
Open the preview strip: R METAL should be bright red (about 255) and G ROUGH near black for mirror chrome. The colour preview barely moves; that is correct.
In iRacing the paint under a metal part should be near white for chrome to read, so dark colours turn dark chrome. Lighten the colour, or choose Satin Chrome or Metallic.
Press RENDER and Ctrl+R in iRacing.

articles.title: Retro stripes and numbers
articles.summary: The fastest way is to type it in Chat: "retro red white and blue stripes, flat with chrome trim". By hand, build each stripe as a box zone with a solid colour and recolour the numbers that your template already has.
articles.what: Shokker is not a drawing program; it paints your template with materials. Stripes come from zones (a coloured area with a finish), from your template's own art, or from artwork you add as a layer. Numbers are not typed in either: they exist in the template or you add them as a picture.
when: You want a classic racing stripe look.
You want different colours or finishes on stripes and numbers.
how: Fast way: open CHAT and type the look (for example "retro red white and blue stripes, flat with chrome trim"). Refine with "thinner", "make the red orange", "matte". Undo any step.
By hand: for each stripe press + Add Zone, open APPLY AREA, press Draw box and drag a long rectangle along the hood, roof or side on the flat sheet.
Give the stripe zone a base (Gloss is a good start) and set BASE COLOR to Use solid color for the stripe colour. Repeat for the white and the blue.
Add the Pinstripe pattern (thin lengthwise pinstripes) or Chevron under PATTERN for extra detail, and set Paint mode to Blend so it keeps your stripe colour.

Numbers: if your template has a Numbers layer, press the zone icon on that layer and give it a finish, or recolour it with BASE COLOR set to Use solid color. There is no Text button; to add new lettering, place a transparent PNG with + Layer in the layer list and move it with Move (V).
Put the stripes above the body zone in the list so they win. Render and check the CAR view.

One side of the sheet may be upside down relative to the other.

articles.title: A two-tone livery in six zones
articles.summary: Plan the car as six zones: trim, hood, roof, trunk, body, and Everything Else at the bottom as the safety net. Give the body a calm finish and the accents a contrasting one, and keep the strongest finish for one hero area.
articles.what: Two-tone works because zones stack. The zone higher in the list wins where two overlap, so accents sit above the body. Matte body with gloss accents, or satin body with chrome trim, are classic pairs because neighbours differ in shine as well as colour.
when: You want a clean, professional two-colour scheme.
You are not sure how many zones to make.
how: Open your paint. Layered template if you can.
Zone 1, trim or stripes: + Add Zone, PICK COLOR FROM CAR on the stripe colour, BASE a contrast finish such as Gloss or Candy.
Zone 2, hood: APPLY AREA, Draw box over the hood; give it the accent colour and finish.
Zone 3, roof: Draw box over the roof; a second accent or the same.
Zone 4, trunk or rear deck: the same.
Zone 5, body: PICK COLOR FROM CAR on the body colour; BASE Matte or Satin with Use source paint if you want to keep the colour.
Zone 6, Everything Else: leave it at the bottom as the safety net for everything the others did not catch.
Check the preview from a distance, then render. Make sure number and sponsor contrast stays strong.

controls.label: PICK COLOR FROM CAR
controls.effect: Claims pixels by colour.

controls.label: Draw box
controls.effect: Claims an area by rectangle.

tips: One dominant colour (about 60 percent), one accent (30), one trim (10).
Use matte beside gloss, or chrome beside dark, so adjacent areas differ in shine too.
pitfalls: Everything Else above other zones steals their pixels; keep it at the bottom.
More effects is not better; one hero area wins.

deep.heading: Shine contrast
deep.body: Neighbours should differ in shine as well as colour: matte body with gloss accents, or satin body with chrome trim. Use matte beside gloss, or chrome beside dark. One dominant colour (about 60 percent), one accent (30), one trim (10).

deep.heading: Everything Else belongs at the bottom
deep.body: Everything Else above other zones steals their pixels. And more effects is not better: one hero area wins.

articles.title: Colour-shift paint that moves in the sun
articles.summary: Choose a Chameleon or other colour-shift finish for the zone: it brings its own colours, which change with the viewing angle in the sim. Recolour it with Hue Shift, not with a solid colour.
articles.what: Colour-shift (chameleon) finishes are built from a spec map and a colour field that shift as the light and your view change, like real flip paint. The flat colour preview shows one angle only, so judge the effect in iRacing. There are many to choose from, from Amethyst and Arctic to Phoenix and Galaxy.
when: You want a flip or chameleon paint.
You want colours that move in the sun.
how: Make a zone for the body (Remaining, or PICK COLOR FROM CAR on the body colour) and tick Car Paint under RESTRICT TO LAYERS to protect numbers.
Under BASE press Base Material and search for Chameleon. Pick one, for example Chameleon Amethyst, Chameleon Emerald or Chameleon Phoenix.
Leave BASE COLOR on Use finish's own color. A solid colour would flatten it to one colour and lose the shift.
To change the hues, use Hue Shift (-180 to 180) under BASE, plus Saturation and Brightness.
Render and press Ctrl+R. Look at the car in the sim under different light. The preview cannot show the angle change, so the sim is the only real check.
Keep neighbouring zones calm (matte or satin, dark) so the shift is the hero.

tips: Shift equals target hue minus current hue: +150 on green gives purple, not pink.
Pair with a dark satin or matte body zone nearby for contrast.
pitfalls: Do not put sparkle, strong patterns or colour shift directly behind numbers.

deep.body: The flat colour preview shows one angle only. Look at the car in the sim under different light. The preview cannot show the angle change, so the sim is the only real check. Keep neighbouring zones calm (matte or satin, dark) so the shift is the hero.

articles.title: Carbon fibre hood
articles.summary: Draw a box zone over the hood, give it a carbon base or a plain dark base plus the Carbon Fiber pattern, and make the pattern fine (scale below 1.0). The weave is the look.
articles.what: Carbon is a texture, so size is everything. On a whole-car sheet a normal weave looks like a fishing net. Go smaller, and put the weave only on the part you want so the rest of the car stays calm.

Your carbon looks huge or blurry.
how: Press + Add Zone. Under APPLY AREA press Draw box and drag a rectangle around the hood on the flat sheet.

Under BASE press Base Material and choose Hardware: Carbon Handguard (a glossy twill weave under resin) or Carbon Twill Weave (a semi-matte 2 by 2 twill), or a plain dark base such as Gloss and add the weave as a pattern.

Lower Scale (pattern) until the weave looks fine on the car: try 0.5. Base Scale does the same for a base with its own weave.
Optional: add a spec overlay such as Carbon Wet Layup under SPEC OVERLAYS for resin depth. It changes shine only.
Render and compare at 100 percent zoom, not in the small fit-to-window view.

articles.title: Candy colours: how to get depth
articles.summary: Candy is a transparent colour over a polished metallic ground. Pick a Candy base, set the colour yourself, then use Color Depth, Color Flip and Underglow to push the richness.
articles.what: A candy paint looks deep because light passes through tinted clear and bounces off bright metal underneath. In Shokker the Candy bases give you that ground and the controls under BASE give you the tint depth. Pale or metallic grounds make candy glow; dark flat ones make it look black.
when: You want a deep, wet, hot-rod colour.
Your candy looks flat or dark.
how: Make a zone on the area (Remaining or a picked colour) and restrict it to Car Paint if you have a layered template.

Under BASE press Base Material and choose Candy on the Foundation Bases shelf (a polished metallic under the colour you pick, so gold, lime or aqua candy is just a colour choice; Van: Candy Apple is a ready-made candy over silver).
Set BASE COLOR to Use solid color and pick a rich colour. Deep red, cobalt and emerald work best.

Raise Color Depth: 0 is no tint, 15 a glaze, 65 rich (the default), 100 deepest. Color Flip adds a second hue at an angle (90 neighbouring, 180 opposite). Underglow lets the ground coat burn through the brights.
Add depth with a spec overlay such as Gold Flake or Pearl Micro, or pick a Spec preset such as Wet Candy.
Check G ROUGH (low is glassy) and B COAT (16 is the deepest coat) in the preview strip, then render.

articles.title: Edit one thing without touching sponsors
articles.summary: To change only the body, give a zone the Car Paint layer under Restrict to layers, or tell Chat "change the body but leave the numbers alone". Numbers, sponsors and logos then stay exactly as they were.
articles.what: Sponsors and numbers sit on their own layers of a layered template, so a zone that is limited to the body layer never reaches them. Without layers, pick the colour with a low tolerance or draw a box. The AI copilot follows the same rule: it never touches numbers, sponsors or logos unless you name them, and every change has an Undo.
when: You want a new body colour but the same numbers.
A change painted over a logo.
how: Open a layered template. In the layer list check which layer holds the body paint (for example Car Paint).
Press + Add Zone, tick only Car Paint under RESTRICT TO LAYERS, and give the zone the colour and finish.
Or in Chat say "change the body but leave the numbers alone" and check the preview; press Undo under the reply if it is wrong.
On a flat TGA, use PICK COLOR FROM CAR on the body colour with a tolerance of 30 to 45, or Draw box around the body panels. Use Exclude Region to cut out a logo.
If a special finish makes numbers sparkle or dull, open MASK > Advanced spec utilities > Decal Rescue Kit and choose Flat Vinyl, Satin Decal or Gloss Decal.
Render and check the numbers in the CAR view.

controls.label: Decal Rescue Kit
controls.effect: Plain non-metal spec under stamped numbers and sponsors.

tips: A whole-car finish that brings its own colour on a zone without a layer restriction paints over every number and logo.
Select logos and numbers by layer name for exact edges; use colour for big flat areas.

Name the decals if you want the AI to change them; otherwise it leaves them.

articles.title: A gradient from blue to gold to white
articles.summary: Put the gradient on the zone that owns the big body area: BASE COLOR, Custom gradient, then three colour stops and a direction. Remember the fade runs across the whole flat sheet, not along the car.
articles.what: A zone can fade between 2 to 10 colours. If the zone only covers some colours of the paint, the gradient shows only there.
when: You want a fade from one colour through a second into a third, such as blue to gold to white.
You want a sunset, fade-out or ombre look on the body.

Add three stops: deep blue at 0, gold at 50 and white at 100 (the stop positions run from 0 to 100).
Choose the direction that matches the flat layout: horizontal runs left to right across the sheet, vertical top to bottom, or one of the diagonal and radial options.
Look at the preview. If one side of the car fades the wrong way, give each side its own zone with its own gradient.

articles.what: A livery pops when neighbouring areas differ in both colour and shine, not when everything gets more saturated. One glossy deep area beside a flat area reads as depth on the car, and a light flake across the body adds sparkle in the sun.
when: The car looks flat or samey.
You want one clear change that lifts the whole design.
how: Find the biggest area and the two colours that contrast most.
Give one of them a deep, glossy candy or pearl of its own colour with BASE COLOR set to use your paint.
Keep the other area matte or satin, or give it a chrome trim.
Add a subtle flake overlay on the body with + ADD SPEC OVERLAY, Strength 30 to 50.
Compare with the SOURCE view and stop when it reads clearly at arm's length.

controls.effect: A faint flake adds sparkle without changing the colour.

tips: Opposite colour and opposite shine beside each other is the strongest contrast.
Change one thing at a time so you can undo it cleanly.
pitfalls: Too many glossy areas cancel each other out. Keep one hero area.

articles.title: Put a race number on your car
articles.summary: Shokker has no box to type a car number. Either let iRacing stamp your number (tick Sim-Stamped Number) or put your own number art on the paint as a layer and tick Custom Number.
articles.what: A race number reaches the car in one of two ways. Sim-Stamped Number: Shokker writes car_<ID>.tga and iRacing stamps the number (and its sponsors) on top, which is what iRacing does when Hide Car Numbers is OFF. Custom Number: the number is part of your paint, Shokker writes car_num_<ID>.tga, and iRacing uses that file only when Hide Car Numbers is ON. Your own number is a picture: if your template is a layered PSD it may have a Numbers layer you can recolour (not every paint has numbers drawn), and a new number is added as a transparent PNG with + Layer in the layer list. There is no Text button in the main tool row.
when: You want a number on the doors, roof or hood.
You want iRacing to put your league number on for you.
You see the number twice or not at all.
how: 1. Decide who draws the number. Let iRacing do it: tick Sim-Stamped Number next to your iRacing User ID at the top. Draw it yourself: tick Custom Number.
2. Your own number: if your PSD has a Numbers layer, press the zone icon on that layer and give it a colour with BASE COLOR set to Use solid color, or a finish.

3. A new number: make it as a transparent PNG (or in your PSD), open the layer list in the right column and press + Layer, then place it with Move (V) and size it with Transform (Ctrl+T) in LAYER mode.
4. In iRacing set Graphics > Hide Car Numbers to match: ON for Custom Number, OFF for Sim-Stamped Number.
5. Render, then press Ctrl+R in iRacing to reload the paint.

controls.effect: Your paint carries the number; writes car_num_<ID>.tga.

controls.label: Sim-Stamped Number
controls.effect: iRacing stamps the number on top; writes car_<ID>.tga.

tips: Only one of the two boxes can be on; clicking the ticked one does nothing.
Put the number zone above the body zone in the zone list so it wins.
pitfalls: Seeing the number twice means a number-stamp layer of the template was left visible while iRacing also stamps one.
Shokker cannot read iRacing's Hide Car Numbers setting; if they disagree iRacing shows your paint-shop colours instead.

put a number on my car

deep.heading: Two files, one setting
deep.body: The two boxes only choose the file name. Custom Number writes car_num_<ID>.tga and Sim-Stamped Number writes car_<ID>.tga. iRacing picks between them with its own Graphics > Hide Car Numbers switch: ON loads car_num_<ID>.tga, OFF loads car_<ID>.tga. Shokker starts with Custom Number ticked.

deep.heading: Where a number picture comes from
deep.body: Shokker paints colours, finishes and spec onto pixels that already exist; it does not type letters. A number is therefore a picture: the Numbers layer of your template, or a transparent PNG you add with + Layer. Once it is a layer you can move, size, recolour it and give it its own finish like any other layer.

faq.a: Tick Sim-Stamped Number to let iRacing stamp it, or add your own number picture with + Layer in the layer list and tick Custom Number.

faq.q: Where do I type my car number?
faq.a: Nowhere in Shokker. The number either comes from iRacing (Sim-Stamped Number) or from number art on your paint (Custom Number).

faq.q: Can I change the colour of the numbers on my template?
faq.a: Yes. Press the zone icon on the Numbers layer and set BASE COLOR to Use solid color, or give it a finish.

faq.q: Why do I see two numbers?
faq.a: A number-stamp layer of the template was left visible while iRacing also stamps one. Hide that layer or switch to Custom Number with Hide Car Numbers ON.

articles.title: Tri-coat, forged carbon, anodized, blackout trim and bug splatter: getting those looks
articles.summary: Tri-Coat Pearl, Forged Carbon Visible, Forged Composite, Anodized, Blackout, Blackout Ops and Rally Mud are real finishes, but none of them is listed in the Base Material picker: ask the AI copilot for them by name. Bug splatter has no finish of its own; Rally Mud and wear are the nearest.
articles.what: Shokker's finishes carry names, so a look you know from a real car is often one request away. These particular looks are real finishes but are not listed in the Base Material picker, so you reach them by asking the AI copilot (or Chat) for them by name. Tri-Coat Pearl is a three-stage pearl: a pale pearl white with fine sparkle and a faint colour shift. Forged Carbon Visible is charcoal with broad organic fibre swirls under a wet clearcoat; Forged Composite is its quieter relative, close to plain dark charcoal with faint marbling and a satin sheen. Anodized is a gritty, matte, deep-blue dyed metal. Blackout and Blackout Ops are murdered-out flat blacks, which is what blackout trim is made of. There is no bug-splatter finish: Rally Mud is a dark charcoal-brown coat with dry mud spray and dirt splatter, matte and stage-worn, and wear adds chips and a duller clearcoat. Anything a finish cannot do, such as real bug marks, can be painted as artwork on a layer. If you would rather stay inside the picker, the nearest listed finishes are Pearl and Satin Pearl, Matte and Flat Black (Foundation shelf), and Forged Carbon, Anodised and Anodized Titanium (type the name in the picker search).
when: You know the name of a look from a real car and want it on yours.
You searched the finish picker for a name such as Tri-Coat Pearl or Blackout Ops and it was not there.
You want trim, grilles or badges blacked out.
how: 1. Make or pick the zone for the area (whole body, or only the trim or hood). A new zone lands at the bottom of the zone list.
2. Open the AI panel (the AI button at the bottom right of PRO, or CHAT at the top) and ask for the finish by name, for example "put Forged Carbon Visible on the hood" or "Blackout Ops on the trim".
3. Look at the preview and the AI's answer; press Undo under the answer if it is not what you wanted.
4. For your own colour on Anodized, set that zone's BASE COLOR to Use solid color and pick the colour; the gritty Anodized otherwise keeps its own deep blue.
5. Render and check it in iRacing; flat blacks and forged carbon read very differently in sunlight than in the preview.
tips: Blackout trim is a zone, not a finish setting: put Blackout or Blackout Ops on a zone that covers only the trim, then drag that zone's handle (the three-line icon in the ZONES column) above the body zone so it wins.
pitfalls: Searching the Base Material picker for these names finds nothing, because the picker does not list them; ask the AI panel by name instead.
The gritty Anodized repaints the area with its own deep blue; set BASE COLOR to Use solid color when you want another colour.
Rally Mud is a whole-coat look, not single bug marks; for a few splats, paint them on a layer.

deep.heading: Which name is which finish
deep.body: Tri-Coat Pearl: a pale pearl white with fine sparkle and a faint colour shift. Forged Carbon Visible: charcoal with broad organic fibre swirls under a wet clearcoat. Forged Composite: a darker, quieter forged look, almost plain dark charcoal with a satin sheen; its marbling is faint at car scale. Anodized: a deep, matte, gritty dyed-metal blue with no sparkle. Blackout: a flat, near-total-absorption black. Blackout Ops: near-flat black with a fine chalky texture. Rally Mud: dark paint with a dry mud spray, matte and stage-worn.

deep.heading: Why you ask by name
deep.body: The Base Material picker lists only part of the finish catalogue. Finishes it does not list can still be applied by name through the AI panel, Chat or the MCP tools. When no finish carries a brand name, search the picker for the material instead (pearl, carbon, anodised, matte), then steer the colour with the zone's hue, saturation and brightness. Effects that are really artwork, such as bug marks, stickers or a hand-drawn graphic, belong on a layer: paint them in your PSD or with the RETOUCH brushes and give that layer its own zone.

faq.q: Is there a tri-coat pearl?
faq.a: Yes, Tri-Coat Pearl exists, but it is not listed in the Base Material picker: ask the AI panel for it by name. The nearest listed finishes are Pearl and Satin Pearl on the Foundation shelf.

faq.q: Can I get forged carbon?

articles.title: Glow-in-the-dark and light-up paint: what is possible
articles.summary: A paint cannot give off light: iRacing has no glow-in-the-dark or emissive paint, and the spec map's lighting mask can only turn lighting down. For a glowing look, put a bright finish such as Arcade: Phosphor Green, Bioluminescent Wave or Firefly Lantern on a dark ground.
articles.what: Shokker writes two pictures for iRacing: the paint (colours) and the spec map (metal, roughness, clearcoat and a lighting mask). None of them can make the car light up at night. The lighting mask in the spec's alpha only decides how much of iRacing's own lighting a spot gets: 255 is normal and 0 switches the lighting response off, which makes a spot look flat, not lit. What you can do is fake a glow with colour and contrast: very bright small shapes on a very dark ground read as glowing. Several finishes are built that way, for example Arcade: Phosphor Green (tiny lime phosphor grains with an emerald afterglow), Arcade: Vector Glow (cyan, violet and hot-pink wireframe fragments), Bioluminescent Wave (ocean bioluminescence with electric-blue wave glow) and Firefly Lantern (light-organ modules that glow like a firefly). For artwork, Layer Effects has an Outer Glow that draws a soft halo round a layer.
when: You want a paint that glows in the dark or lights up at night.
You want neon or UV-looking paint.
You want a logo or number with a glowing edge.
how: 1. Make a zone for the area (+ Add Zone; use APPLY AREA to draw a box if it is only part of the car).
2. Under BASE press Base Material and type glow, phosphor or neon in the search box.
3. Pick a glow finish such as Arcade: Phosphor Green, Arcade: Vector Glow, Bioluminescent Wave or Firefly Lantern and keep BASE COLOR on Use finish's own color.
4. Keep the rest of the car dark: glow looks only read against black or deep navy.
5. For a glowing logo or number, select its layer, press STROKE FX on the layer card and tick Outer Glow, then Apply.
6. Render and check it in iRacing at night and in daylight; it will look painted, not lit.
tips: Keep the bright parts small; a whole car in neon green looks pastel, not glowing.
Outer Glow size runs from 1 to 50 and opacity from 0 to 100; a small size reads as a crisp neon edge.
pitfalls: Setting the lighting mask (alpha) to 0 does not make a spot glow: it removes the lighting response, so the spot looks flat.
Glow finishes bring their own colours; switching BASE COLOR to a solid colour can lose the glowing contrast.
aliases: make my car glow at night

deep.heading: Why a paint cannot glow
deep.body: iRacing lights the car itself: sun, sky and track lights. The paint says what colour each spot is and the spec map says how metal, rough and glossy it is. There is no channel that adds light, so no file Shokker writes can make the car shine on its own in the dark.

deep.heading: How the glow finishes fake it
deep.body: Glow finishes put small, very bright shapes on a near-black field. Your eye reads a bright spot next to black as a light source, the same way neon signs look in photos. They look strongest at night and on dark cars, and calmer in bright sun.

faq.q: Can I make a glow-in-the-dark paint?
faq.a: No. iRacing has no emissive paint. Use a bright glow finish on a dark ground for the look.

faq.q: Does setting the alpha or lighting mask to zero make it glow?
faq.a: No. Zero switches iRacing's lighting response off for that spot, so it looks flat and unlit.

faq.q: Which finishes look like they glow?
faq.a: Search glow, phosphor or neon in Base Material: for example Arcade: Phosphor Green, Arcade: Vector Glow, Bioluminescent Wave and Firefly Lantern.

mistakes.symptom: The area turned flat and grey in iRacing.
mistakes.cause: The lighting mask was set to 0 there.
mistakes.fix: Put the alpha back to 255; use a glow finish for the look instead.

protips: Pair one glow colour with black and nothing else: cyan or lime on black reads as light from across the track.

articles.title: Number fonts and number style
articles.summary: Shokker has no font or text tool for numbers. With Sim-Stamped Number iRacing draws the number in its own style; for your own font, make the number as a transparent PNG in another editor, add it with + Layer and tick Custom Number.
articles.what: A race number reaches the car in one of two ways. Sim-Stamped Number writes car_ID.tga and iRacing stamps the number on top in its own style; Shokker has no setting for that font. Custom Number writes car_num_ID.tga and the number is part of your paint, so it can be any font you like, but you make the number art outside Shokker: there is no Text button in the main tool row. Add the finished number as a transparent PNG with + Layer, place it with Move (V) and Transform (Ctrl+T), and give it an outline or shadow with Layer Effects (STROKE FX on the layer card). iRacing loads car_num_ID.tga only when its Hide Car Numbers option is ON.
when: You want a different font for your race number.
The stamped number does not match your design.
You want an outlined or shadowed number.
how: 1. Decide who draws the number: iRacing (Sim-Stamped Number) or you (Custom Number), next to your iRacing User ID at the top.
2. Your own font: type the number in Photoshop or another editor in the font you want and save it as a transparent PNG.
3. In Shokker open the layer list, press + Layer and pick the PNG; place it with Move (V) and size it with Transform (Ctrl+T) in LAYER mode.
4. For an outline or shadow, press STROKE FX on the layer card, tick Stroke or Drop Shadow and Apply.
5. Tick Custom Number, render, and set Hide Car Numbers ON in iRacing's graphics settings (restart iRacing after changing it).
tips: Make the number art large; scaling a small PNG up makes it blurry.
pitfalls: With Sim-Stamped Number on, iRacing adds its own number; do not also paint one.
Custom Number with Hide Car Numbers OFF means iRacing finds no file and shows paint-shop colours.

deep.heading: Two ways, two kinds of font
deep.body: Stamped numbers are iRacing's: they follow iRacing's own number style, and Shokker only chooses the file name that tells iRacing to stamp. Custom numbers are artwork in your paint, so any font you can type in a photo editor works, as long as you bring the number in as a picture.

deep.heading: Making number art that looks sharp
deep.body: Type the number big, export it as a transparent PNG, and size it down in Shokker rather than up. Outlines and shadows from Layer Effects stay editable, so you can change their colour later without remaking the number.

faq.q: Can I change the font of my number in Shokker?
faq.a: Not with a font menu. Make the number in your font as a transparent PNG and add it with + Layer, then tick Custom Number.

faq.q: Which font does a sim-stamped number use?
faq.a: iRacing's own number style; Shokker has no setting for it.

faq.q: Can I outline my number?
faq.a: Yes: Layer Effects (STROKE FX) adds a stroke or drop shadow to the number layer.

mistakes.cause: You painted a number and Sim-Stamped Number is on.
mistakes.fix: Tick Custom Number and set Hide Car Numbers ON in iRacing, or remove your painted number.

mistakes.cause: A small PNG was scaled up.
mistakes.fix: Export the number art larger and scale it down in Shokker.

protips: Keep the number art on its own layer with its effects; recolouring or moving it later is then one step.
